strengths: Addresses an underexplored and well-motivated problem: existing LLM-based SDG agents focus on deduction/strategy selection but largely ignore the persuasive, listener-directed dimension of communication.

The Stackelberg framing provides an intuitive and reasonably systematic way to operationalize 'persuasion' as a concrete, differentiable training objective (shifting a follower's response distribution), rather than relying on vague notions of eloquence.

Broad empirical coverage: experiments span three structurally different SDGs (Werewolf, Avalon, ONUW), multiple state-of-the-art baselines per game, and consistent improvements are shown when the trained Refiner is combined with each baseline.

Useful ablations, including a reward-decomposition study (positive-only vs. negative-only vs. combined) that yields an interpretable finding (asymmetry between rewarding desired vs. penalizing undesired responses), and a two-stage vs. single-stage / prompt-only refinement ablation that supports the necessity of RL fine-tuning over pure prompting.

Demonstrated generalization of the trained Refiner to unseen backend LLMs (GPT-5, Qwen3-14B) without retraining, suggesting the learned refinement is not merely overfit to training-time backend styles.
The plug-in design (refining any baseline's utterance) is practically appealing and simplifies integration with prior work.
weaknesses: The core reward signal is questionable: persuasive impact is measured as the log-probability that a frozen open-source Measurer (a copy of the Refiner's own base model) generates an exact pre-specified target utterance, given the candidate utterance. This is a very indirect, high-variance proxy for whether a real follower (often a different, API-based LLM) would actually adopt the desired stance—paraphrased but semantically equivalent responses would receive low reward, and there is no validation (e.g., correlation analysis) showing that this Measurer-based reward tracks actual behavior changes in the real, heterogeneous follower models used at evaluation time.

There is an unaddressed train/test mismatch: during training, the reward computation is given the follower's hidden role rt+1 ('we leverage full information during training'), while at inference this information is unavailable to the leader when identifying intent. The paper does not analyze how much this discrepancy affects the quality/realism of the learned reward or the resulting policy.

No human evaluation of persuasiveness or naturalness of the refined utterances; all evidence of effectiveness is indirect (win rate in self-play among LLM agents), which conflates 'persuasion' with any property that happens to move specific opponent LLMs (e.g., verbosity, assertiveness, or exploiting quirks of particular models) rather than demonstrating genuine, generalizable persuasive skill.

The 'theoretical foundation' (Stackelberg competition, Appendix B) is largely narrative/motivational rather than a rigorous formalization—there is no derivation of an optimal leader strategy, no equilibrium analysis, and no formal connection between the stated mathematical objective (Eq. 13) and the actual GRPO training procedure beyond analogy.

Reproducibility concerns: several baselines and the agent pool depend on closed, versioned commercial APIs (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-3.5-Haiku, GPT-5) without fixed snapshots/dates, which are subject to silent updates and access restrictions, undermining exact replicability of the reported win rates.

Statistical rigor is limited: win-rate differences (e.g., ONUW Ours+ReAct 44.3% vs. ReAct 43.6%) are reported as single point estimates from 500 matches with no confidence intervals or significance testing, making it hard to assess whether some reported gains are meaningful versus noise.

It is unclear whether baseline methods were run under identical conditions/backends as claimed in the original papers or reimplemented by the authors, and whether the 'Ours + Baseline' comparison is entirely fair (e.g., baselines are not also given access to the same refinement infrastructure or an equivalent parameter/compute budget).
The case studies (Appendix E) are hand-picked qualitative anecdotes rather than systematic analysis, and offer limited evidentiary weight for the claimed sophistication of persuasive strategies.

strengths: Addresses an under-explored and interesting angle in LLM-agent SDG research: optimizing for persuasive impact on other players rather than purely strategic/deductive reasoning.

The two-stage architecture (API-based backend for base utterances + trainable open-source LoRA refiner) is a practical engineering solution to the problem of not being able to fine-tune closed-source models, and is compatible with existing baselines as a plug-in module.
Reasonably broad empirical scope: three different SDGs (Werewolf, Avalon, ONUW), an ablation on reward components, and a cross-model generalization test (GPT-5, Qwen3-14B) not used during training.

Qualitative case studies (Appendix E) give some intuition for the kind of linguistic strategies the refiner learns (e.g., referencing prior behavior, directing conversational flow to a target player).
weaknesses: The 'Stackelberg competition' framing is largely a rebranding exercise rather than a substantive theoretical contribution: there is no formal leader/follower optimization, no equilibrium computation, and no derivation connecting the stated game-theoretic objective to the actual training loss beyond a restated RL objective (Eq. 13). Appendix B, despite its length, consists mainly of narrative/psychological assertions (Elaboration Likelihood Model, social proof, commitment/consistency) with no formal grounding, inflating the paper's apparent rigor without adding real analytical content.

A central soundness concern: the reward signal (Eq. 5) is computed using a frozen 'Measurer' that is simply a copy of the same open-source LLM used for the Refiner, NOT the actual follower/opponent, which in both self-play data collection and evaluation is an API-based LLM (GPT-4o/Gemini/Claude/baseline agents). This creates a potentially large mismatch between the proxy reward model and the real follower whose behavior the method claims to be shaping, undermining the core claim that the agent is learning to model and influence 'the follower's response distribution.'

The reward itself (next-token log-likelihood of a hypothetical target utterance under the Measurer, conditioned on inserting ut into context) is a weak and indirect proxy for persuasion; it could reward surface priming or lexical overlap rather than genuine argumentative influence, and this is never directly validated (e.g., no correlation analysis between reward and actual observed shifts in real opponents' behavior).

Evaluation relies entirely on aggregate win-rate differences from relatively small samples (50-500 matches per condition) with no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance testing, despite SDGs being highly stochastic (role assignment, voting ties, LLM sampling). Several reported gains are only a few percentage points (e.g., Avalon good-side win rate unchanged for Ours+Strategist vs. Strategist, 77.9 vs 77.9), making it hard to distinguish real effects from noise.

The main results table (Table 1) uses a pooled heterogeneous-agent evaluation design where many different agent types (including the proposed method's multiple variants) compete simultaneously with varying participation counts; this introduces confounds in attributing performance differences specifically to the proposed persuasive-refinement mechanism versus other sources of variance in the player pool.

No human evaluation or any direct assessment of 'persuasiveness' as perceived by evaluators is conducted; the paper equates win-rate improvement with successful persuasion, but these outcomes are also influenced by role-specific strategic competence, random pairing, and other uncontrolled game factors.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: training hyperparameters are given, but the self-play dataset (500 logs/game) and exact backend prompting pipeline are not clearly released, and there's no mention of code/data availability, limiting independent verification of the reported results.

strengths: Identifies and addresses a genuine gap in prior LLM-for-SDG work, which largely reduces communication to selecting from a finite candidate/action space; this paper instead optimizes free-form natural-language utterances directly for persuasive impact.

The Stackelberg framing gives a clean, implementable training signal (shift in probability of eliciting a desired vs. undesired next-player response), operationalized via a practical GRPO-based refinement pipeline that is agnostic to the backend LLM.

Reasonably broad empirical scope: three distinct SDGs (Werewolf, Avalon, ONUW), integration with multiple existing baselines (ReAct, ReCon, SLA, LSPO, LASI, Strategist, Belief/LLM-ins./RL-ins.), an ablation on reward components (positive-only vs. negative-only vs. combined), a two-stage vs. direct-training ablation, and a cross-backend generalization study (GPT-5, Qwen3-14B).

The 'plug-in' design (refining another agent's base utterance rather than replacing the whole pipeline) is a practically appealing contribution that could generalize to other multi-agent dialogue settings.
Illustrative case studies give some qualitative insight into what the refined utterances actually do (e.g., building coalitions, directing conversational flow to a target listener).
weaknesses: The core reward signal relies on an open-source 'Measurer' LLM estimating the likelihood that a closed, different-architecture API model (GPT-4o/Gemini/Claude) would produce an exact target utterance; there is no validation that this proxy correlates with real follower behavior, which undermines the soundness of the entire training signal.

No statistical significance testing or variance/seed reporting anywhere; many comparisons (especially ablation and generalization tables) are based on only 50 matches per condition, and several 'Ours' improvements over baselines in Table 1 are only a few percentage points, making it unclear whether reported gains are robust versus noise.

Training uses privileged information (the next player's true hidden role) that is unavailable at evaluation time; the paper does not empirically analyze the resulting train/test mismatch or how much this inflates apparent gains.

Both 'intent identification' (desired/undesired responses) and reward computation rely entirely on LLM judgment with no human validation that identified targets are actually strategically sound, so the entire pipeline could be optimizing toward the backend model's biases rather than genuinely 'persuasive' or game-optimal content.

The Stackelberg 'theoretical foundation' (Section 3.1 and Appendix B) is mostly descriptive/motivational rather than rigorous game theory; it does not provide formal optimality guarantees, and the connection between the local one-step objective and actual game outcomes is argued qualitatively rather than proven or empirically decomposed.

Baseline reproductions (SLA, LSPO, Strategist, etc.) are re-run under the paper's own chosen backend LLMs and experimental harness, raising reproducibility/fairness concerns since these methods may have been tuned for different original setups.

Overall claims of 'significant' improvement and 'model-agnostic principles of persuasion' are somewhat overstated given the absence of significance tests and the reliance on a small number of matches and cherry-picked qualitative case studies.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely underexplored angle in LLM agents for social deduction games: optimizing utterances specifically for their persuasive effect on the next speaker's response, rather than just role deduction or discrete strategy selection.

The proposed reward (log-probability shift toward desired vs. away from undesired follower responses) is a concrete, differentiable operationalization of 'influence' that can be trained with GRPO without a critic or human preference data.

Very extensive empirical validation: four distinct environments (Werewolf, Avalon, ONUW, Sotopia) plus an additional bargaining benchmark (AmazonHistoryPrice), multiple backend LLMs (including held-out GPT-5 and Qwen3-14B for generalization), several ablations (reward-function variants, K sweep, dataset-size sweep, two-stage refinement necessity), and a human-subject evaluation with real Werewolf players.

The 'Ours + Baseline' plug-in design (refining any existing baseline's utterances) is a practical contribution demonstrating that the method is complementary to prior strategy-selection approaches rather than a replacement.

Reasonably detailed prompts, implementation details (LoRA rank, GRPO hyperparameters, compute budget) and case studies are provided, aiding reproducibility and interpretability of what the refiner learns.
weaknesses: The 'Stackelberg competition' framing is mostly rhetorical/intuitive rather than a rigorous game-theoretic formalization; Appendix B offers narrative justification but no formal equilibrium concept, best-response characterization, or proof that the local pairwise optimization approximates a meaningful global solution—so the theoretical contribution is thinner than the framing suggests.

The reward is computed using a fixed proxy 'Measurer' (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct) to simulate the follower's response distribution, which differs from the actual (often proprietary) backend LLMs used as opponents at both training and test time; this proxy-follower mismatch is not deeply analyzed and could bias the learned persuasive strategies toward exploiting proxy-model idiosyncrasies rather than genuine persuasion.

Reward computation during training uses privileged information (the next player's true hidden role) that is unavailable at inference, creating a train/test information asymmetry whose impact on policy quality and potential overfitting is not investigated.

No variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for any win-rate results, despite relatively modest sample sizes (50–500 matches) and some reported gains that are numerically small (e.g., ONUW Ours+ReAct overall 45.1 vs. 43.1); this weakens confidence in the robustness of the claimed improvements.

Evaluation relies substantially on LLM judges (e.g., Gemini-2.5-Flash) and on backend LLMs from the same families used elsewhere in the pipeline, raising potential self-preference/evaluator bias concerns that are not discussed or controlled for.

Human evaluation is limited to a single game (Werewolf), a small uncompensated volunteer pool (16 students), and does not report inter-rater agreement or demographic/skill controls, limiting generalizability of the human-AI results.

The paper notes but does not experimentally address the observed increase in utterance length during training, an important confound since longer, more elaborate utterances could partly explain persuasive gains independent of the proposed Stackelberg mechanism.

strengths: The paper tackles an underexplored but legitimate problem: optimizing persuasive utterances (rather than just role inference/strategy selection) in social deduction games.

Broad empirical coverage: three SDGs (Werewolf, Avalon, ONUW) plus Sotopia and an additional bargaining benchmark (AmazonHistoryPrice), with the proposed Refiner shown to be pluggable on top of multiple existing baselines.

Reasonably thorough ablations: reward-function variants (positive-only vs negative-only vs combined), sensitivity to K, training-data-size scaling, and cross-backend generalization to models not seen during training (GPT-5, Qwen3-14B).
Includes a human-subject evaluation (16 participants playing Werewolf against/with the agents), which is uncommon and adds some ecological validity.
Reasonably reproducible implementation details (LoRA rank, GRPO hyperparameters, prompts in appendix) and qualitative case studies that illustrate the intended mechanism.
weaknesses: The 'Stackelberg competition' framing is largely rhetorical: no actual leader-follower equilibrium, utility matrices, or formal game-theoretic derivation is used; Appendix B is prose-level justification rather than a rigorous theoretical contribution, so the 'theoretical foundation' claimed in the abstract and contributions is overstated relative to what is delivered.

The reward signal depends entirely on a single frozen surrogate 'Measurer' (Qwen2.5-72B) to estimate the response probability of followers that are, at both training and test time, often different and more capable closed models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude, GPT-5, Qwen3-14B). The validity of this proxy as a stand-in for diverse real followers is asserted rather than rigorously validated (e.g., no correlation study between Measurer-predicted shifts and actual behavior change of the true backend LLMs beyond the main win-rate outcomes).

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting (confidence intervals, multiple seeds) across the 500-match evaluations, despite large and sometimes dramatic win-rate swings (e.g., Werewolf Village 17.5%→29.1%, ONUW Werewolf 40%→50.6%); it is hard to judge whether these differences are robust or an artifact of a single run/sampling.

Potential reward-hacking confound: the stated limitation that trained utterances become longer directly interacts with the log-probability-sum reward (Eq. 5), since longer/more elaborate utterances can shift token-level log-likelihoods of the appended target response for reasons unrelated to genuine persuasive content (e.g., more context, more hedging tokens). This confound is acknowledged only as a stylistic 'limitation' rather than analyzed or controlled for.

The heterogeneous 500-match tournament setup (random sampling of agent types per role) introduces confounds the paper itself flags ('overall win rate is not a simple average, as agents are more frequently assigned to the majority faction') but does not fully disentangle; it is unclear how much of the reported gain is attributable to the Refiner itself versus interaction effects of role assignment frequency across heterogeneous pools.

Training reward relies on privileged information (true hidden roles of the follower) that would not be available at inference, and the measured probability of desired/undesired responses is computed via the same model family generating the 'ground truth' targets — raising concerns about circularity between intent identification, reward computation, and the trained objective.

Related work and discussion are relatively thin on connections to the broader NLP/computational-pragmatics literature on persuasion and argumentation outside of game agents, making the novelty claim relative to that literature underexplored.

The hybrid two-stage architecture (closed API backend + fine-tuned LoRA refiner + separate frozen Measurer for training signal) adds non-trivial computational and engineering overhead that is not discussed in terms of cost or latency trade-offs, limiting practical assessment of the contribution's efficiency.

strengths: Novel and intuitive theoretical framing: casting turn-based SDG dialogue as a Stackelberg leader-follower game gives a principled way to operationalize 'persuasion' as an optimizable, differentiable reward (shift in follower's response log-probability), moving beyond prior work that reduces communication to discrete action/strategy selection.

Very thorough empirical evaluation: results span three distinct SDGs (Werewolf, Avalon, ONUW) plus a fourth open-ended social simulation (Sotopia) and an additional bargaining benchmark (AmazonHistoryPrice), with consistent, non-trivial improvements over multiple strong baselines in each.

Extensive and well-designed ablations: reward-function components (positive-only vs negative-only vs both), K hyperparameter sweep, training data size, and a careful comparison against prompt-based (non-trained) refinement baselines that convincingly shows the necessity of the RL training step rather than mere prompting.

Strong generalization tests: the trained Refiner (fine-tuned on GPT-4o/Gemini/Claude self-play data) transfers to unseen backend LLMs (GPT-5, Qwen3-14B) without retraining, and the method is shown to be plug-and-play with other existing baselines (LSPO, Strategist, RL-ins., MetaMind), improving over each.

Human evaluation with real players in Werewolf is a valuable and relatively rare addition, showing the trained agent both wins more and draws fewer suspicious votes, supporting real-world applicability claims.
Clear writing, detailed appendices with prompts, game rules, and case studies that aid reproducibility and qualitative understanding of what the refinement is doing.
weaknesses: The reward signal depends on a fixed open-source 'Measurer' (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct) as a proxy for the actual follower's (API-based, possibly different-model) response distribution. This proxy-model mismatch is a core soundness concern that is only indirectly addressed via cross-model generalization experiments rather than directly validated (e.g., by measuring correlation between Measurer-predicted shifts and actual follower behavior).

During training, the reward computation uses the follower's ground-truth hidden role, which is unobservable to the leader at inference/in the real game; while the authors note this is meant to produce 'more accurate' rewards, it introduces an information asymmetry between train and test that is not carefully analyzed for potential bias or overfitting effects.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting (e.g., across seeds/multiple runs) is provided for the main win-rate comparisons, despite some deltas being modest (a few percentage points) in certain settings; this makes it hard to assess robustness of the smaller reported gains.

The 'theoretical' analysis in Appendix B is largely discursive/motivational rather than a rigorous formal game-theoretic derivation (no proofs, no formal equilibrium concept applied to the language setting), so the Stackelberg framing functions more as a useful heuristic/narrative than a formally validated model.

Potential evaluation circularity: Gemini-2.5-Flash is used simultaneously as a backend LLM in training data generation, as a default backend for many evaluations, and as the LLM judge for Sotopia, raising a possible self-favorability concern that is not explicitly controlled for.

The acknowledged tendency of the Refiner to produce longer utterances is a real confound: increased length could mechanically improve probability-based persuasion rewards or similarity-to-target metrics independent of genuine persuasive quality, and this is not disentangled through a length-controlled ablation.

Human evaluation involves only 16 unpaid volunteer students with self-selected interest in the game, limiting demographic diversity and possibly introducing selection bias; the human study is also restricted to Werewolf only, not extended to the other games/environments.
